hints: Hooke’s law states a proportional relationship.
Name the two quantities and the condition that limits the relationship.
walkthrough: Hooke’s law applies only in the proportional region of a force–extension relationship.
State that extension is proportional to applied force, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.

ai_rubric.observable: States that extension is proportional to applied force, or an equivalent Hooke's-law statement.

hints: The proportional region is the straight-line section through the origin.
Locate the point where the graph first stops being straight, then place P on the line.
walkthrough: A material obeys Hooke’s law where force is proportional to extension, shown by a straight line through the origin.
The line first departs from this straight section at extension 60 mm and force 5.4 N.
Place and label P at (60 mm, 5.4 N).

ai_rubric.observable: Places P on the curve at approximately 60 mm extension and 5.4 N.

hints: The question states the maximum extension for elastic behaviour.
Find 80 mm on the extension axis, move to the graph line, and label that point E.
walkthrough: The elastic limit is the greatest extension from which the sample still recovers its original length.
The stem states that the sample behaves elastically up to 80 mm.
At 80 mm the graph force is about 5.9 N, so place and label E at (80 mm, 5.9 N).

ai_rubric.observable: Places E on the curve at approximately 80 mm extension and 5.9 N.

hints: Use a point from the straight-line part of the graph, before P.
Convert the extension from millimetres to metres before finding the force–extension gradient.
Use k = F / x with F = 5.4 N at x = 0.060 m.
walkthrough: Within the proportional region, k = F / x and is the gradient of the force–extension graph.
At P, F = 5.4 N and x = 60 mm = 0.060 m.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses k = F/x or the gradient of the straight-line graph region.
Uses 5.4 N and 0.060 m consistently to obtain 90 N m⁻¹.

hints: Young modulus can be written E = FL / (AΔL), or as kL/A in the proportional region.
Convert 0.40 mm² to 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m² and 60 mm to 0.060 m.
Use a force and extension from the straight-line section of the graph.
walkthrough: Use E = FL / (AΔL) with F = 5.4 N, L = 3.2 m, A = 0.40 mm² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m², and ΔL = 0.060 m.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses Young modulus as stress divided by strain, E = FL/(AΔL), or the equivalent kL/A.
Substitutes the graph force or spring constant, length, area and extension with consistent SI conversions.

knowledge_refs.formula_empty_justification: The required estimate is the area under a non-linear force–extension graph, rather than application of a single controlled major formula.

hints: Work done is represented by the area beneath a force–extension graph.
Break the area to the breaking point into simple approximate shapes or count grid squares.
Remember to convert the horizontal axis from millimetres to metres when expressing the area in joules.
walkthrough: For a force–extension graph, the work done is the area under the graph because each narrow strip represents force multiplied by a small extension.
Estimate the areas of the linear, nearly level and rising sections up to X, converting the extension scale to metres.
The total graphical area is about 1.0 J; estimates from 0.8 J to 1.2 J are acceptable.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that the work done is the area under the force–extension graph.
Obtains an area estimate of about 1.0 J within the accepted graphical range.

hints: The two samples have the same material, so their Young modulus is unchanged.
Use E = kL/A and note that the original length is also unchanged.
Decide how k must change when A increases while E and L remain fixed.
walkthrough: For the same material, Young modulus E is unchanged, and the samples have the same original length L.
Rearranging E = kL/A gives k = EA/L.
A larger cross-sectional area gives a larger spring constant, so a greater force is needed for the same extension.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that increasing cross-sectional area reduces extension for a given force, increases required force for a given extension, or gives k proportional to area.
States that the second sample has a greater spring constant.
